I watch and listen.
I watch him through the days as he settles into his ways.
I listen when the captain sings his wild sea-songs.
I listen to his stories.
I follow Dr. Livesey into the parlour.
I watch the captain and the doctor.
I watch the doctor and the captain.
I lay the breakfast-table against the captain's return, then ask the stranger what he wants.
I tell him I do not know his mate Bill, and that the table is for our captain.
I step out into the road once, and am slow to come back when he calls me.
I wait behind the door where the stranger puts me, and watch.
I fetch Black Dog's rum, then retire into the bar and try to listen.
"Are you hurt?" I cry, and I run to fetch the rum.
"Oh, doctor," I cry, "what shall we do? Where is he wounded?"
I help the doctor hoist the captain upstairs to his bed, and listen to his warning.
I take cooling drinks and medicines up to the captain at noon.
"I want none of your money," I say, "but what you owe my father. I'll get you one glass, and no more."
"Black Dog?" I ask.
I give him his medicine.
I watch him.
"You are at the Admiral Benbow, Black Hill Cove, my good man," I say, and hold out my hand to him.
I warn him the captain sits with a drawn cutlass, then lead him in and cry, "Here's a friend for you, Bill."
I obey the blind man and take the captain's left hand by the wrist, bringing it near to the man's right.
I tell my mother everything I know.
I go with my mother to the hamlet and tell the villagers our troubles.
I tell my mother I will go back with her, and take the loaded pistol the villagers give me.
I go down on my knees beside the captain's body.
I hold Mrs. Crossley's bag for my mother.
"Mother," I say, "take the whole and let's be going."
"And I'll take this to square the count," I say, and pick up the oilskin packet.
I creep back to the bank and hide my head behind a bush of broom to watch the road.
I stay behind the broom, listening to the inn.
I listen to the men's voices and watch them from my hiding place.
I watch the scene unfold from my hiding place.
I stay in my hiding place and watch.
I leap to my feet and hail the riders.
I go back with Mr. Dance to the inn, and tell him I believe I have in my breast pocket the thing the men were after.
I ride behind Dogger to Dr. Livesey's house, knock, and ask the maid, "Is Dr. Livesey in?"
I watch and listen.
"Here it is, sir," I say, and I give him the oilskin packet.
I listen to them from the side-table.
I peer over the doctor's shoulder at the book.
I watch and listen.
I watch the doctor.
I listen to the squire and the doctor.
I stay on at the hall with old Redruth, brooding over the map, and open the letter that comes for the doctor.
I read the squire's letter, and tell Redruth, "Dr. Livesey will not like that. The squire has been talking, after all."
I continue reading the letter.
I finish reading the letter, postscript and all.
I walk with Redruth to the Admiral Benbow to see my mother.
I say good-bye to my mother and the cove, ride the mail with Redruth, and wake to ask, "Where are we?"
I walk with Redruth along the quays, looking at the ships, then cry, "Oh, sir, when do we sail?"
I carry the squire's note to the Spy-glass tavern and hang at the door, afraid to go in.
I walk right up to the man and hold out the note, asking, "Mr. Silver, sir?"
"Dog, sir," I say. "Has Mr. Trelawney not told you of the buccaneers? He was one of them."
"That he did, you may be sure," I say. "I knew that blind man too. His name was Pew."
I listen to Silver, and join in his laughter.
I join his laughter, then walk with him along the quays to the inn.
I bear out what Long John says, then go aboard the Hispaniola with the squire and the doctor.
I go down into the cabin with the squire and the doctor.
I listen.
I keep listening.
I keep listening to the captain.
I listen to the conversation and then follow them out onto the deck.
I help change the powder and the berths.
I examine the long brass swivel amidships, and hurry off to the cook for work.
